claim: `akasha change apply` starts a whole-repository typecheck without asking the admission guard, and nothing bounds how many applies run at once. The guard already exists and already works: it refuses a dev-server, a seat spawn and a supervisor child while the machine is short of memory. Apply is not one of its three callers, so the number of concurrent whole-repository typechecks is the number of agents that happen to be landing, and each one holds several gigabytes.

evidence:
THE INSTANCE. 2026-09-13 at 15:55, with thirteen agents landing at once: 13 `akasha change apply` processes, 13 `tsc` processes holding 16.0 GB between them, and 141 `bun` processes holding 19.6 GB. Of 62 GiB the host had 332 MiB free, 49 GiB in use, and 54 GiB of 79 GiB of swap taken, with zram full at 16G of 16G. /proc/pressure/memory read `some avg10=69.88 full avg10=57.31`, so every task on the machine was stalled waiting on memory 57 per cent of the time. No kernel OOM kill and no oomd kill fired; the swap absorbed it, which is why the machine went slow rather than dying. Forty minutes later, with the applies drained to one, the same readings were load 18.28 and `some avg10=3.51`.

THE GUARD HAS THREE CALLERS AND APPLY IS NOT ONE. Read 2026-09-13, every call site of both entry points in `util/system/modules/memory-guard/memory-guard.module.code.ts`:
  dev-server-running.module.code.ts:95        enforceMemoryGuard(KIND)
  spawn-seat.module.code.ts:99                enforceSpawnAdmission(worker name)
  supervisor-child-spawn.module.code.ts:37    admitSpawn: given.admitSpawn ?? enforceMemoryGuard
Nothing under `command/` calls either. `MIN_FREE_MEMORY_GB` is 8 and the host had 12 GiB available at the worst of it, so the guard would not have refused these applies at that threshold either; what it would have done is be on the path at all.

WHY A CAP IS POSSIBLE HERE. Apply is one command with one entry point, so it can hold a lock or ask the guard before it starts a typecheck. The two findings already filed about memory are about ceilings on processes already running and about limits not being page properties; neither says which commands ask for admission. `every-ceiling-the-reaper-holds-sits-above-what-a-runaway-agent-reaches` records that admission is the part that works and that it bounds nothing already running. This is the other side of that: the most expensive thing an agent starts does not pass through it.

NOT MEASURED. What one apply costs on its own, and how many can run together before the machine is worse off than running them in turn.
